newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW-Japan loan cleanup body faces tough task.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Japan loan cleanup body faces tough task.

text.p: A year after Japan passed a controversial law to clean up the mess left by failed "jusen" mortgage firms, the body charged with carrying out the task has managed to recover a hefty chunk of loans.

But despite the progress made so far, the Housing Loan Administration Corp (HLAC) concedes it faces a stiff challenge to recover remaining assets in a timely fashion and minimise the burden of the "jusen" debacle on the nation's taxpayers.

The possibility of higher interest rates, which will increase the body's funding costs, the fragile real estate market and obstruction from underworld figures linked to jusen borrowers are possible stumbling blocks, the HLAC's president said in a recent interview with Reuters.
The HLAC was set up last July as a subsidiary of the Deposit Insurance Corp of Japan, a quasi-governmental body which protects depositors in the event of bank failures.

Under the law, the HLAC aims to recover the jusen loans over a period of 15 years. If it is left with losses, taxpayers must pay for half of the future losses and financial institutions the other half.
HLAC president Kohei Nakabo said in the interview that the corporation is determined to recover the loans in seven and a half years, without asking taxpayers to pay more.

He said they had got off to a good start, collecting 275.6 billion yen ($2.41 billion) of loans in the business year which ended on March 31 and expecting to collect another 160 billion yen ($1.40 billion) in the first quarter of fiscal 1997/98.

"If the collection goes as planned, we should be able to achieve the target of collecting 630 billion yen in loans in the current business year," said Nakabo, a former chairman of the Japan Federation of Bar Associations who has 40 years' experience as a lawyer.

"Banks, managers at the mortgage firms and the Finance Ministry are responsible for the jusen problem. Taxpayers were forced to help settle the issue, although they did not do anything wrong," he said.
It was in June last year that the cleanup plan became law after months of haggling in parliament about using public money to sort out a private-sector problem.

After the law was passed, 680 billion yen ($5.96 billion) of taxpayers' money was used to help write off 6.4 trillion yen ($56.1 billion) of problem loans at the failed jusen firms. Banks and other financial institutions contributed 5.73 trillion yen ($50.2 billion) to help in the cleanup.
Then the remaining jusen assets totalling 6.1 trillion yen ($53.5 billion), including problem loans, were transferred to the HLAC under the scheme.
Nakabo, 67, said it was essential to apply principles of fairness and transparency to loan-collecting.
"We should not make any compromise with borrowers whose hands are dirty. Cutting ties with the underworld is also important to be fair in collecting problem loans," he said.

Jusen lent heavily for property deals during Japan's bubble economy of soaring land and share prices in the latter half of the 1980s. But many of the loans soured after the bubble burst and the mortgage firms buckled under the weight of the debt.
Authorities have admitted that many of the loans were linked to gangsters, or "yakuza", making collection a particularly daunting task.
Nakabo said that the HLAC, in cooperation with police, has brought nine criminal cases and several civil actions against gangsters who had occupied buildings taken over by the loan-collecting body.

Japanese financial institutions have made loan-loss provisions for problem loans but have been reluctant to recover the money for fear of interference or revenge by gangsters, he said. But gangsters who are owed money by jusen borrowers are vigorous in pursuing the debtors and are not keen to see the money pass to the HLAC, causing security concerns for the loan-collecting body, he said.

Despite the success so far, Nakabo said he was worried about the prospect of rising interest rates, which would increase costs on the HLAC's own borrowings. In addition, recovering collateralised property will also be tough as real estate prices have fallen rapidly, he said.
He also said he intends to look at who was responsible for the jusen mess.
After a heated debate over whether jusen managers should be held accountable, the cleanup measures adopted last year fudged the question of responsibility for the loan fiasco.
"It would not contribute very much to our loan collection business, but we must make it clear who was responsible for the mess," he said. ($1=114 yen)
